draft.title: Culture and scientific knowledge
card: People in every culture have built knowledge of the natural world. Much of it comes from careful observation over a very long time.
First Nations Australians have lived on and cared for Country for tens of thousands of years. They hold detailed knowledge of plants, animals, seasons, weather and land.
This knowledge is passed on through stories, songs, art and practice. Each generation checks it against what they see, and adds to it.
Culture can shape what science studies. A community's knowledge and concerns can lead scientists to ask new questions, and the two can work together.
draft.remember: Many cultures build knowledge by long observation, and their views can shape the questions science asks.

a.q: How have First Nations Australians built knowledge of plants, animals and seasons?
opts: Through careful observation over a very long time
Through guesses that were never checked again
Through experiments done only in modern laboratories
Through copying ideas from other countries' scientists
a.why: The knowledge comes from watching Country closely over many generations, and each generation checks it against what they see. It was not built in modern laboratories, and it was not unchecked guesswork.
a.clue: Think about how long people have lived on Country.

b.q: Scientists in northern Australia ask a local Aboriginal ranger group about the timing of seasons. The rangers' knowledge leads to a new study of when plants flower. What does this show?
opts: A community's knowledge can shape what science studies
Only laboratory scientists can come up with useful questions
Cultural knowledge replaces the need to observe anything
Seasons are the same in every part of Australia
b.why: The rangers' knowledge led scientists to ask a new question, so culture shaped what was studied. The card says the two can work together, so it does not replace observation, and it does not mean that only laboratory scientists ask good questions.
b.clue: Which option is about where the scientists' question came from?

a.best: Through careful observation over a very long time

b.best: A community's knowledge can shape what science studies

problems.detail: Distractors use absolute words ("done only in modern laboratories", "never checked again"). The card speaks in terms of what can happen. These absolutes make the wrong options easy to rule out without knowing the idea.
The distractor "Only laboratory scientists can come up with useful questions" uses "only", while the card says culture "can" shape science. The absolute makes it easy to eliminate on wording alone.

proposal.title: Culture and scientific knowledge
card: People in every culture have built knowledge of the natural world. Much of it comes from careful observation over a very long time.
First Nations Australians have lived on and cared for Country for tens of thousands of years. They hold detailed knowledge of plants, animals, seasons, weather and land.
This knowledge is passed on through stories, songs, art and practice. Each generation checks it against what they see, and adds to it.
Culture can shape what science studies. A community's knowledge and concerns can lead scientists to ask new questions, and the two can work together.
proposal.remember: Many cultures build knowledge by long observation, and their views can shape the questions science asks.

a.q: An Aboriginal group knows that a certain plant flowering signals a change of season. Where did this knowledge most likely come from?
opts: Watching Country closely over many generations
Recording flowering dates for a single season
Tests run in a university laboratory
Books written by scientists from overseas
a.why: First Nations knowledge of seasons comes from close observation of Country, passed on and checked by each generation over a very long time. One season of records is too short to build this kind of knowledge, and it did not come from laboratories or overseas books.
a.clue: Think about how long people have lived on Country.

b.q: Scientists in northern Australia ask a local Aboriginal ranger group about the timing of seasons. The rangers' knowledge leads to a new study of when plants flower. What does this show?
opts: A community's knowledge can shape what science studies
Science questions come from labs, not from communities
The rangers' knowledge makes the flowering study unneeded
Cultural knowledge is a separate topic from science
b.why: The rangers' knowledge led scientists to ask a new question, so culture shaped what was studied. The study still went ahead, which shows the two working together rather than one making the other unneeded.
b.clue: Where did the idea for the flowering study come from?
